extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, journalists, and researchers interested in U.S. censorship law and media policy
extracted.subtask_description: An encyclopedic overview of U.S. censorship across media (broadcast, film, internet, print) describing legal standards, landmark cases, statutes, and historical/industry self-regulation that shape what may be published or broadcast. Useful for readers wanting the legal and historical criteria that govern speech restrictions in the United States.

rubrics_metrics.name: FCC indecency rules / fleeting expletives policy
rubrics_metrics.description: The FCC has the power to keep "indecent" material off the airwaves from 6 a.m. to 10 p.m.; it can sanction and fine broadcasters for indecency (with maximum fines noted between US$268,500 to US$375,000 per incident). The FCC's policy on so-called fleeting expletives was upheld as not "arbitrary or capricious" in procedural terms by the Supreme Court in FCC v. Fox Television Stations, Inc. (2009), though the constitutional question was remanded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples cited include Bono's use of "fucking brilliant" at the Golden Globes and on-air uses by Cher and exchanges involving Paris Hilton and Nicole Richie. The Supreme Court majority (Scalia) justified regulation to give "conscientious parents a relatively safe haven for their children"; dissenting justices criticized the policy as vague and shifting. Enforcement is time‑of‑day limited (6 a.m.–10 p.m.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadcast time‑of‑day safe harbor for indecency
rubrics_metrics.description: For 30 years the FCC has had the power to keep 'indecent' material off the airwaves from 6 a.m. to 10 p.m.; these rules define a time window when broadcasters may be restricted from airing indecent content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes that these rules "have not proved unworkable" (Justice Stevens dissent argued), and that enforcement and definitions of indecency have been contentious and litigated.

rubrics_metrics.name: First Amendment protection for motion pictures (historical shift)
rubrics_metrics.description: Historically, motion pictures were regarded as commerce and not as protected speech (Mutual Film Corporation v. Industrial Commission of Ohio, 1915), but the Supreme Court reversed that view in Joseph Burstyn, Inc. v. Wilson (1952), holding films entitled to First Amendment protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Between those decisions local and state censorship boards exercised broad power to edit or ban films; Joseph Burstyn reduced the threat of government regulation and undermined the studio-era Production Code's legal justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Production Code / MPAA film approval (industry self‑regulation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Hollywood Production Code (aka Hays Code / Production Code) and later the Production Code Administration (PCA) required films to obtain a certificate of approval before release; the industry enforced a set of 'don'ts and be carefuls' and a moral system for content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Code was not government law but studio self-regulation intended to avoid federal censorship. The PCA could require cuts and refusal of approval kept films out of theaters; over time enforcement loosened and the Code was abandoned as studios released films without approval and social mores changed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obscenity vs. indecency; child pornography exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: U.S. courts have ruled that the First Amendment protects 'indecent' pornography but not 'obscene' pornography; child pornography is unlawful and not protected (New York v. Ferber).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State v. Henry (Oregon) abolished obscenity under the Oregon Constitution (not federal). Ashcroft v. Free Speech Coalition (2002) held that virtual child pornography (produced without actual minors) can be protected unless obscene. The federal PROTECT Act (2003) and 18 U.S.C. §2252A criminalize realistic computer-generated depictions indistinguishable from actual minors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 230 immunity for interactive computer services
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 230 provides that 'No provider or user of an interactive computer service shall be treated as the publisher or speaker of any information provided by another information content provider,' shielding platforms from liability for third‑party content and for good‑faith content moderation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The protection is often called 'the First Amendment of the Internet.' It also contains limits: it 'does not apply to federal criminal law, intellectual property law, and electronic communications privacy law' (per EFF). Section 230 shields platforms so long as moderation is done in 'good faith', though critics argue platforms may still perpetuate harmful rhetoric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Congressional limits on online facilitation of prostitution / FOSTA/SESTA
rubrics_metrics.description: FOSTA/SESTA (Stop Enabling Sex Traffickers Act / Allow States and Victims to Fight Online Sex Trafficking Act) made it illegal for an interactive computer service to promote or facilitate prostitution and lifted civil and some criminal immunity for facilitation of sex trafficking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enacted in 2018, supporters argued it targeted sites like Backpage; critics say it endangered sex workers and led platforms to self‑censor (e.g., Craigslist removing personals). FOSTA/SESTA was litigated on First Amendment grounds and was upheld by a D.C. circuit court in July 2023.

rubrics_metrics.name: Travel Act criminalization of interstate promotion of unlawful activity
rubrics_metrics.description: The Travel Act makes it illegal to 'promote, manage, establish, carry on, or facilitate the promotion, management, establishment, or carrying on, of any unlawful activity' across state lines, used in prosecutions related to online platforms facilitating prostitution (e.g., Backpage).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department of Justice used Travel Act counts in the 2018 seizure and indictment of Backpage.com executives; the Act can be applied to cross‑state online facilitation of illegal conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Library and institution internet filtering precedent (U.S. v. ALA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts have held that private entities (businesses, schools, libraries, government offices) may use filtering software to censor at their discretion; U.S. v. ALA (2003) permits libraries to filter internet content under certain statutory schemes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The ruling is limited to its facts and specifically to libraries; it does not automatically apply to private businesses or platforms. The article references related case law (e.g., Marsh v. Alabama) and notes complexity around which entities the decision covers.

rubrics_metrics.name: National Security Letters (NSLs) and gag orders
rubrics_metrics.description: NSLs are administrative demands for information issued by the federal government without prior judicial review and accompanied by gag orders preventing recipients from revealing the NSL existence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics contend NSLs prevent public oversight and allow unreasonable search and seizure to go unchecked. The ACLU challenged expansions of NSL power (e.g., changes by Section 505 of the USA PATRIOT Act) that allowed broader demands and gagging of recipients not connected to terrorism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior restraint and injunctions to block publication
rubrics_metrics.description: The government has used prior restraint—court injunctions or other prohibitions—to prevent publication of material (e.g., United States v. The Progressive temporarily blocked an article purported to reveal hydrogen bomb details).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior restraint cases are historically significant in censorship debates; sometimes temporary injunctions are sought on national security grounds, but publication may later occur if similar information is published elsewhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invention Secrecy Act / withholding patents for national security
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the Invention Secrecy Act of 1951 and the Atomic Energy Act of 1954, patents may be withheld and kept secret on grounds of national security.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article cites historical examples (e.g., Scientific American copies destroyed after an article on thermonuclear fusion) and notes that the government can impose secrecy orders on patent applications for national security reasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrictions on publishing weapons‑making instructions (Feinstein amendment)
rubrics_metrics.description: A 1997 amendment (Feinstein amendment) to a Department of Defense spending bill forbids distribution of instructions that teach 'the making or use of an explosive, a destructive device, or a weapon of mass destruction' if those instructions are intended to assist in actual building or use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The restriction targets intent to assist actual construction/use; it was added to prevent dissemination of operational instructions for dangerous devices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Export controls on cryptography and source code as speech
rubrics_metrics.description: Export of cryptography software has been regulated as a munition under ITAR, though regulations have relaxed; litigation (Bernstein v. United States) held that software source code is speech protected by the First Amendment, constraining publication restrictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes that while some regulations have relaxed due to industry lobbying, some export controls on cryptography remain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embedding journalists and wartime reporting constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters embedded with military units are often obliged to accept constraints on reporting via contracts, punishment, relocation, and the reliance on the military unit for protection and presence, limiting what they may report from battlefields.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article describes embedding as a mechanism that can limit independent reporting; wartime censorship can involve surveillance and contractual constraints that affect journalists' ability to report freely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trading/anti‑boycott restrictions under the Trade Agreements Act (TRA) / EAR
rubrics_metrics.description: A 1977 law penalizes U.S. persons for supporting the boycott of Israel when that boycott is originated by a foreign nation or organization; the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) lists conduct that may be penalized under the TRA and/or prohibited under the EAR.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conduct that may be penalized includes agreements to refuse business with Israel or blacklisted companies, discrimination based on protected categories, furnishing information about business relationships or about race/religion/sex/national origin, and letters of credit with prohibited boycott terms. The TRA penalizes material participation in foreign-originated boycotts but does not prohibit purely domestic political speech supporting a boycott.
